title: Staged weight activation and checkpoint commit protocol
content:
Purpose and scope:

This doc defines the "Staged Weight Activation" workflow and a small, deterministic "Checkpoint Commit Protocol" for serving-runtime weight updates. It targets the following use cases: lazy-loading large model shards from disk (safetensors or mmap-able artifacts), performing background validation, and atomically switching the live inference graph to a new checkpoint without introducing transient inconsistency or large latency spikes. This is complementary to our residency/eviction controller and differs from prior drafts by emphasizing a multi-phase activation state machine with automatic rollback, signed artifact verification, and probabilistic warmup probing to avoid cold-start latency cliffs.

Goals:
- Provide an atomic, observable activation boundary for checkpoint swaps (so in-flight requests either fully use old weights or fully use new weights).
- Allow progressive background materialization (decompress/quantize/convert) without blocking request threads.
- Support on-disk mmap of safetensors as a zero-copy read path when available, with fallback to memory-backed shards when mmap is not possible (e.g., remote FS).
- Ensure safety: checksum + manifest verification, model ABI compatibility checks, and deterministic rollback when activation fails.
- Keep runtime memory bounded via configurable residency caps and staged eviction of old weight pages.

Key concepts and terminology:
- checkpoint: a logically versioned collection of weight shards (safetensors, pt/onnx exports, or quantized tiles).
- shard: a file-sized artifact containing weights for a set of layers (commonly aligned to module boundaries).
- materialization: the process of transforming an on-disk shard into runtime-ready memory (mmap mapping, quantized kernel packing, or GPU-transfer-ready buffers).
- activation: the single point where the serving runtime switches the inference graph to reference the new checkpoint state.
- staging area: per-worker local storage/state where in-progress materialization lives prior to activation.
- probe request: a small synthetic or sampled real request used to warm up caches/KV and validate outputs after activation.

High-level workflow (phases):
1) Intake and verification (controller):
   - Controller receives a checkpoint manifest (signed, includes shard list, sizes, checksums, ABI version, compatible runtime versions, and optional precomputed mmap offsets).
   - Verify signature and checksums. If verification fails, reject artifact and emit error metric CHECKPOINT_VERIFY_FAIL.

2) Reservation and placement (controller + scheduler):
   - Controller consults residency policy and per-node capacity to select candidate nodes for staged activation.
   - Reserve disk/memory budget for staging area (max_staging_mb). Reservation can be soft; controller retries if insufficient resources.

3) Staged materialization (worker local):
   - For each shard, attempt materials in order: 1) open as read-only mmap if filesystem supports it and manifest lists mmap offsets; 2) decompress into memory-mapped temp (memory-backed) with standard page-aligned layout; 3) full load into JVM/GPUMemory buffers if kernel requires packing/transpose/quantization.
   - Each materialization step is asynchronous and returns a promise/future. Workers materialize low-latency-critical shards first (attention, embeddings) using priority list embedded in manifest.
   - During materialization, maintain a per-shard state: pending -> mapped -> validated -> ready. Validation includes checksum and lightweight value-range checks for known pathological models.

4) Dry-run validation and compatibility checks (worker):
   - Run a small set of deterministic probes using internal canary prompts (or sampled low-cost live requests if allowed). Compare output signatures/stats to expected lightweight heuristics (token distribution, softmax sanity checks). If check fails, mark shard as BAD and notify controller.

5) Activation commit (atomic switch):
   - Once all critical shards are READY, the controller initiates activation. Activation is a two-phase local commit per worker:
     - Phase A (prepare): publish new checkpoint handle to local routing table but keep live inference graphs pointing to old weight handles. Install indirection layer entry mapping model_id -> {old_handle, new_handle, activation_state: pending}.
     - Phase B (commit): on a locally synchronized epoch boundary (safe points include: request quiescence, end-of-step hooks, or after draining finite inflight ops), atomically swap the inference graph pointer to new_handle. This swap must be single-instruction atomic on pointer/reference under our runtime to guarantee no mixed reads.
   - Metric: ACTIVATE_LATENCY measured from commit request to first successful response using new weights.

6) Post-activation warm-up and probe traffic:
   - Immediately after commit, route a small percentage of traffic through measurement hooks to collect output quality and latency telemetry. If behavior drifts outside configured thresholds (e.g., perplexity jump or token distribution anomalies), automatically trigger rollback.

7) Graceful teardown of previous checkpoint:
   - After a configurable grace period (default 5 minutes), the old checkpoint enters EVICTABLE state. Eviction occurs in a staged manner: unreleasable pages (pinned KV cache, on-going GPU tensors) are drained first, then cold pages are unmapped or freed.

Failure modes and rollback:
- Partial materialization failure: mark checkpoint as INVALID, do not proceed to activation; alert operator.
- Probe mismatch after activation: immediate rollback to previous handle and flag checkpoint for manual review. Ensure rollback path can be executed even if some old shards were paged out — old shards must be retained until grace period expires.
- Node-restart during activation: on startup, detect any checkpoint in pending/activating state and reconcile with controller; either finish activation atomically if materialized, or roll back and requeue.

Mmap specifics and fallback behavior:
- Prefer mmap when: file resides on local disk or network FS that supports mmap semantics and manifest includes stable file inode/offset metadata. mmap path is zero-copy for CPU inference; for GPU kernels we still require a copy into pinned device buffers but mmap can speed up host pre-processing and sharded reads.
- Fallback: if mmap fails (EMFILE, ENOMEM, unsupported FS), transparently fall back to read-into-memory buffer. Emit metric MMAP_FALLBACK with reason.
- Page residency hints: when mapping, use madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL or MADV_WILLNEED) heuristics based on layer access patterns known from the manifest (e.g., embedding tables often require random access). For remote filesystems, use a conservative read-ahead and staged async prefetch worker to avoid blocking the main materialization pipeline.

Safetensors handling and verification:
- Manifests must include per-shard safetensors header digest and field-level signatures where available. During materialization, we perform an initial header parse and length sanity check before any large mmap or read. For compressed safetensors (e.g., zstd), decompress into staging temp files and then optionally reserialize to aligned safetensors to enable mmapping on next activation.
- To reduce repeated decompression costs, store a compact page-index manifest alongside the decompressed artifact to allow partial re-mmap on next activation.

KV cache and pinned pages interplay:
- KV cache pins a subset of activations and past key/value tensors. During activation, we must ensure pinned KV pages remain consistent. Strategy: upon commit, maintain dual-KV mapping for a short window where new requests write into the new KV while reads for older in-flight ops continue to reference old KV. After grace period and safe drain, consolidate hot KV entries into new KV (copy-on-write) and release old pinned pages.
- Expose per-model sticky_kv_threshold that controls how aggressively pinned pages are migrated vs retained. This helps avoid thrashing on high-QPS models with large context windows.

APIs and operator commands (controller -> worker):
- POST /checkpoint/intake {manifest_url, signature, model_id, priority} -> intake_id
- POST /checkpoint/intake/{id}/reserve {node_list, max_staging_mb} -> reservation_id
- POST /checkpoint/reservation/{id}/materialize {node} -> async task id
- POST /checkpoint/{id}/activate {model_id, rollout_pct, probe_config} -> activation_id
- POST /checkpoint/{id}/rollback {reason} -> immediate/queued
- GET /checkpoint/{id}/status -> {phases: list, node_states: list}

Data model (simple strings/lists only in this doc):
- manifest fields: name, version, shards[], checksums[], abi_version, priority_layers[], signed_by
- shard descriptor: path, size_bytes, compressed(boolean), mmap_offsets(optional), preferred_load_strategy

Observability and metrics:
- CHECKPOINT_VERIFY_FAIL, CHECKPOINT_MATERIALIZE_TIME, MMAP_FALLBACK, ACTIVATE_LATENCY, ACTIVATE_ROLLBACk_COUNT, PROBE_MISMATCH_ALERTS, STAGING_CAPACITY_SHORTAGE
- Tracing: activation is a trace-span that joins controller + worker events. Include shard-level spans for long materialization ops.

Security and integrity:
- All checkpoints must be signed by authorized model-onboarding keys and validate against org root. Support key-rotation via manifest signed_by chain.
- Enforce immutable manifest semantics: once a checkpoint is activated, the identity hash of shards is recorded in audit logs and must match subsequent controller references; mismatches are treated as tampering.

Testing and validation plan:
- Unit tests for state transitions + simulated partial failures (disk full, mmap fail, corrupted shard).
- Integration smoke: 1) cold activation of 8B and 70B models on a single node with and without mmap. Measure peak memory and ACTIVATE_LATENCY. 2) Canary rollout: progressive activation with 1/10/50/100% traffic split and automated rollback on probe mismatch.
- Chaos tests: kill worker mid-materialize, restart controller, ensure deterministic reconciliation.
- Performance benchmarks: measure throughput and p99 latency during activation for different sizing of staging MB and grace period.

Operational runbook (short):
- Alert CHECKPOINT_VERIFY_FAIL: check signature authority and re-upload artifact.
- Alert MMAP_FALLBACK high rate: inspect FS health and inode exhaustion; consider increasing file descriptor limits or switching to streaming strategy.
- Alert PROBE_MISMATCH_ALERTS: immediately pause rollout, inspect output diffs and open SR with ML team.

Open questions and TODOs:
- Decide default grace period: 5 minutes vs 30s for aggressive environments.
- Define compact on-disk page-index format for decompressed safetensors to ease future mmap.
- Explore kernel-friendly packing format that avoids a secondary copy for GPU fast-paths.
- How to support partial-shard hot-swap when only quantized tiles change?

References and related docs:
- RFC-2024-weight-residency-controller (conceptual overlap)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842 (activation hooks prototype)
- JIRA SRV-1273 (hot-swap incidents post-deploy)

Notes to reviewers:
- This spec intentionally keeps activation semantics strict to avoid mixed-weight reads. If we relax atomicity later (for ultra-low-latency ops) the staged model will support gradual exposure but will require further KV consistency guarantees.

-- Maya
